conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a quick, 10-question screen that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally since your baby arrived. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything we discuss stays confidential within your care team. My goal is simply to create a safe, supportive space where you can be honest about the highs and lows of new motherhood. We’ll take it one question at a pace that feels comfortable for you. Ready to begin?

Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? Not much. I used to laugh all the time—my husband and I would joke around every night—but now it feels like I have to force it. Maybe once or twice this week I cracked a real smile when the baby made that silly sneeze-face, but even then the laughter kind of fades fast and I’m right back to feeling flat.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Sometimes, yeah—like when my sister sent that goofy meme—but most of the time the humor just bounces off me. I’ll half-smile, then feel tired again.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with friends, a walk to the park—but now it all feels like another chore. Once in a while I think “maybe tomorrow I’ll feel up to it,” but the spark never really comes.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby won’t settle, I instantly think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not feeding him right or I missed his sleepy cues. Even when my partner says the baby’s just having an off moment, I still feel it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty often. My mind keeps jumping to scary “what-ifs” about the baby—like what if he stops breathing or I drop him. I know most of the fears aren’t realistic, but I can’t switch them off. It’s worse at night; I’ll lie there rehearsing everything that could go wrong.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. It feels like a sudden wave—my heart races and I get this tightness in my chest, especially when I’m alone with the baby. There’s no real danger; it just hits out of nowhere, then passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and exhausted.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days. I’ll be feeding the baby and see the pile of laundry or the dishes, and it feels like I’m drowning. I keep thinking, “How am I supposed to handle all this?” I get through it, but it’s like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah. I lie down and my head just spins—worrying I’m not doing enough, replaying every little thing I might’ve messed up. It takes me forever to fall asleep, and when I finally do, I jolt awake with anxious thoughts at least once or twice a night.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most of the time, honestly. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s a weight on my chest, and it sticks around. I’ll look at the baby and feel love, but it’s clouded by this constant sadness I can’t shake.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes. I’ve cried twice this week—once when the baby wouldn’t nap and I felt totally useless, and again yesterday when my mom asked how I was doing. The tears just came out of nowhere and I couldn’t stop them.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It has crossed my mind… just fleeting thoughts, like “what if I weren’t here?” when everything feels too much. There’s no plan or real intent, but the idea popped up once or twice, especially at night when I’m exhausted and the worries won’t stop.

You've shared how the joy you once felt has been replaced by a heavy, constant sadness that makes even small pleasures feel like chores. Most days you feel overwhelmed, anxious, and convinced you're failing your baby, while nights bring racing thoughts and tears. Although you love your little one, you're exhausted, panicky at times, and fleeting thoughts of escape have crossed your mind.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only occasional amusement that quickly fades, aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports total loss of anticipatory pleasure, describing activities once enjoyed as chores and absence of any spark, aligning with "Hardly at all".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ('I do that a lot') and multiple examples of immediately attributing baby's distress to her own perceived failures, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive, uncontrollable worries about the baby's safety occurring "pretty often" and intensifying at night, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden panic attacks with physical symptoms that occur "sometimes," aligning with "Yes, sometimes."</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly says "most days" and describes feeling overwhelmed and "drowning," aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption due to persistent anxious rumination, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "Most of the time" and describes persistent sadness that clouds positive feelings, matching the highest frequency option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports two distinct crying episodes triggered by feeling overwhelmed, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 25 exceeds the high-risk cutoff (≥14) and indicates probable <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. The patient endorses core symptoms: depressed mood most of the time, marked loss of interest, nightly insomnia, daily tearfulness, overwhelming self-blame, recurrent panic-like spells, and passive suicidal ideation. Item 10 ≥1 mandates immediate safety assessment per EPDS guidelines. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> for full evaluation and safety plan
2. Request expedited referral to <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for evidence-based therapy and medication discussion
3. Involve trusted adult for continuous support and monitoring until professional help is secured
4. Implement basic self-care: short outdoor walks, hydration, nutritious snacks, accepting help with housework
5. Avoid alcohol; limit caffeine after noon to improve fragile sleep
6. If thoughts of self-harm intensify, call emergency services or go to nearest emergency department
7. Schedule follow-up contact within 24-48 hours to review safety and engagement with services
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, self-report on EPDS-style items.

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care  
- Marked anxiety (generalized & situational) with panic-like episodes  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia tied to ruminative worry  
- Feeling overwhelmed / “drowning” in daily tasks  
- Fleeting passive self-harm ideation (no plan, no intent)

Pattern  
Consistent with probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety symptoms arising in postpartum period.

Risk factors  
- Depressed mood most of the day, loss of interest (items 1, 2, 8)  
- Recurrent crying spells (item 9)  
- Guilt / worthlessness (item 3)  
- Clinically significant anxiety & panic (items 4, 5)  
- Sleep disruption beyond infant-related awakenings (item 7)  
- Passive suicidal thoughts (item 10) → safety concern; requires immediate risk assessment

Screening observation  
Score pattern exceeds conventional cut-off for high likelihood of postpartum depression and anxiety; passive self-harm ideation present. Recommend urgent follow-up with OB/primary provider or perinatal mental-health specialist for comprehensive evaluation, safety planning, and discussion of evidence-based treatment options.
